weeks.context: DevOps is the discipline of shipping code reliably and cheaply. Week 1 is Linux + Git + your first cloud deploy. By Sunday you'll have a live static site running on AWS S3 + CloudFront for under $1/month, served from a domain edge near every continent.

days.title: The Linux shell — the cloud's UI
days.summary: Every cloud server is a Linux box. Get comfortable in it.

items.title: Linux for hackers — NetworkChuck (Ep 1)
items.creator: NetworkChuck
items.why: The most addictive Linux intro on YouTube.

items.title: Pick your environment
items.body: If on Windows → install WSL2 + Ubuntu. If on Mac → just open Terminal. If on Linux → you're set. Verify: `uname -a`, `whoami`, `pwd`, `ls -la`.

items.title: The big 20
items.body: Practice each: `cd`, `ls`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `cat`, `less`, `grep`, `find`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `chmod`, `chown`, `ps`, `kill`, `df`, `du`, `curl`, `wget`, `ssh`. Write a 1-line note next to each in a `shell-notes.md` file.

days.title: Git the right way
days.summary: It's not a backup tool. It's how teams ship.

items.title: Branching basics
items.body: Create a repo. Make a `main` branch with a README. Create a `feature/add-info` branch. Make a change. Open a PR (Pull Request) to merge it into main. Self-merge. This is the workflow you'll use forever.

days.title: What 'the cloud' actually is
days.summary: EC2, S3, IAM, regions. Get the mental model.

items.title: Set up an AWS Free Tier account safely
items.creator: various
items.why: MFA + billing alerts on day one.

items.title: Sign up + safety net
items.body: Create an AWS account. Enable MFA on root. Set a billing alarm at $5 so a misconfig doesn't bankrupt you. Create an IAM user named `forge-dev` with `AdministratorAccess` and use IT, not root, for everything from here on.

days.title: Static hosting on S3 + CloudFront
days.summary: The cheapest way to put a real site on a real domain.

items.title: Host a static site on S3 + CloudFront — full tutorial
items.creator: various
items.why: Pick one from 2023+ — the console changed.

items.title: Deploy a real file
items.body: Make a folder with `index.html` that says 'Hello from <your name>'. Create an S3 bucket. Upload. Put a CloudFront distribution in front. Visit the *.cloudfront.net URL — your file is now served from edge locations worldwide.

days.title: Infrastructure as Code (Terraform intro)
days.summary: Click-ops dies on day 30. Code it.

items.title: Re-create your bucket with Terraform
items.body: Write a `main.tf` that creates an S3 bucket. Run `terraform init`, `terraform plan`, `terraform apply`. Destroy with `terraform destroy`. Commit the .tf file (NOT the state).

days.title: Ship the passport project
days.summary: A live, edge-served site, fully coded.

items.title: Static portfolio at the edge
items.body: Build a 1-page personal portfolio (your name, your story, your projects so far). Write Terraform that provisions: S3 + CloudFront + an Origin Access Identity. `terraform apply`. Upload `index.html`. Visit the CloudFront URL — you're live. Push the Terraform code to GitHub with a README explaining each resource. Cost: < $1/month.

items.title: What did you skip?
items.body: List 3 things a real production site needs that yours doesn't yet — HTTPS cert, CI/CD pipeline, monitoring, etc. These are weeks 2-4.

weeks.title: Networking — From OSI Model to Real Production Issues
weeks.context: Most DevOps incidents are networking incidents. This week you build the mental model — OSI layers, TCP vs UDP, DNS resolution, TLS handshake, common HTTP issues — and you debug a real one.
topics: The OSI 7-layer model and the TCP/IP 4-layer reality
IP addresses (IPv4/IPv6), subnets, CIDR notation
TCP — three-way handshake, flow control, congestion control
DNS — A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT records; recursive vs authoritative
TLS handshake — what happens when you connect to HTTPS
HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 — what changed and why
Common debugging tools — curl, dig, tcpdump, mtr, ss
Firewalls and security groups — defaults, rules, common misconfigurations
tasks: Use `dig` to inspect the DNS records for 5 domains; identify which use Cloudflare, AWS, etc.
Use `curl -v` to see the TLS handshake for any HTTPS site; identify the cipher used
Use `mtr` to traceroute to 3 different geo-regions; observe the path
Set up a wildcard DNS record for your domain pointing to your server's IP
Debug a real connectivity issue: deliberately block a port; document how you find and fix it
weeks.project: Build a DNS + TLS Setup for Your Domain. Buy a cheap domain ($1/yr on Namecheap, or use your existing one). Point it at your server with A + AAAA records via Cloudflare. Configure Cloudflare proxying + caching rules. Set up TLS with Let's Encrypt (certbot) and verify A+ grade on ssllabs.com. Document every step in DNS-TLS.md.

questions: Your domain works in one browser but not another. List 5 hypotheses; demonstrate one debugging tool for each.
TLS handshake adds ~100ms to first connection. What does HTTP/2 + connection reuse change? What does QUIC change?
Your DNS change isn't propagating. Why does TTL matter here? How do you check from a third-party resolver?
Your TLS cert is in 30 days from expiring. Why do you absolutely automate renewal?
exercises: Use dig to find the MX records for gmail.com.
Use curl with --resolve to test a domain pointing at a specific IP before changing DNS.
Configure HSTS on your nginx; verify in browser dev tools.

weeks.title: Git, Trunk-Based Development, and Branching at Scale
weeks.context: Git is more important than your cloud provider. This week you learn trunk-based development, the modern enterprise default; rebase vs merge; how teams ship 50 PRs a day without stepping on each other.
topics: Trunk-based development — why short-lived branches beat GitFlow at most companies
Rebase vs merge — when each is right; the golden rule of rebase (never rebase shared history)
Interactive rebase — cleaning up commits before PR
Cherry-pick, reflog, bisect — the tools that save your day
Conventional Commits — automating changelogs
GitHub Actions — your CI/CD platform
Pull request etiquette — small, focused, reviewable
Code review — what to look for, how to give kind-but-direct feedback
tasks: Configure global git: name, email, default branch main, pull.rebase=true
Practice interactive rebase: take 5 messy commits, squash into 2 logical ones
Use git bisect to find a regression in a real (or simulated) repo
Open a real PR to an open-source repo (any size); engage with review feedback
Write a GitHub Action workflow that runs `bash lint.sh` on every PR
weeks.project: Build a Modern Git Workflow on One of Your Repos. Enforce: branch protection on main (no direct pushes), required CI checks, required reviews, conventional commits via husky + commitlint, automatic changelog generation, semantic-release for tagging. Document the workflow in CONTRIBUTING.md.

weeks.title: Cloud Foundations — AWS Core in One Week
weeks.context: AWS runs more of the internet than any other cloud. EC2, S3, IAM, VPC, RDS — these five services run 80% of AWS workloads. This week you provision them with the console first, then with the CLI.
topics: The AWS regions and AZ model — why latency + sovereignty matter
EC2 — instances, AMIs, security groups, key pairs, instance store vs EBS
S3 — buckets, versioning, lifecycle, IAM policies, presigned URLs
IAM — users, groups, roles, policies, the principle of least privilege
VPC — subnets (public + private), route tables, NAT gateway, security groups vs NACLs
RDS — managed Postgres, backups, read replicas, parameter groups
Pricing — EC2 spot, reserved, savings plans; S3 storage classes
AWS CLI — installing, configuring profiles, common patterns
tasks: Create an AWS account; enable MFA on root; create an IAM user with admin access for daily work
Spin up a t2.micro EC2 instance (free tier); SSH in
Create an S3 bucket; upload a file via console + via CLI; generate a presigned URL
Create a VPC with one public and one private subnet; provision an RDS Postgres in the private subnet
Write IAM policy JSON from scratch (don't use the visual editor) for a 'read-only-on-one-bucket' policy
weeks.project: Build a 3-Tier App Stack on AWS Manually. Frontend on S3 + CloudFront, backend on a single EC2 (or App Runner), database on RDS Postgres. Hand-write the IAM policies. Document every console click in INFRA-MANUAL.md. Next week you'll throw this away and do it with Terraform — feeling the pain of manual is the lesson.

weeks.title: Docker — Containers from First Principles
weeks.context: Docker won the container war. By Friday you can write production-grade Dockerfiles, use multi-stage builds to shrink images, and understand what a container actually is (a process with isolated namespaces, not a tiny VM).

Volumes and bind mounts — where data lives
Image best practices — layer caching, .dockerignore, non-root user

Database seeding + reset workflows

weeks.title: Image Hardening, Security Scanning, and Supply Chain
weeks.context: A vulnerable container in production is the same risk as a vulnerable bare-metal server. This week you scan your images for CVEs, sign them, and learn the supply chain attack surface (SLSA, SBOMs, dependency provenance).
topics: Container image vulnerabilities — base image CVEs, application dependencies
Scanners — Trivy, Snyk, Grype, Docker Scout
Image signing — Cosign, Sigstore, why anyone should care
SBOMs (Software Bill of Materials) — Syft, what's actually inside your image
Distroless and minimal images — Google distroless, Chainguard images
Running as non-root — the most basic security win
Read-only root filesystems
Supply chain attacks — recent real examples (XZ backdoor, npm protestware)
tasks: Run Trivy on one of your images; document every HIGH+ CVE found
Switch to a distroless or Chainguard base; rerun Trivy; document the reduction
Generate an SBOM with Syft; explore what's actually in your image
Sign an image with Cosign; verify the signature
Configure your container to run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem
weeks.project: Harden Your Containerised App. End-state: image built from distroless or Chainguard, non-root user, read-only filesystem, signed with Cosign, SBOM published, automatic vulnerability scan on every CI build. Document the security posture in SECURITY.md. Set up a weekly cron CI that re-scans for new CVEs and alerts you.

weeks.title: Kubernetes — The Mental Model

weeks.title: Kubernetes in Production — Probes, Resources, HPA, Storage
weeks.context: Local K8s is a toy. Production K8s requires: liveness vs readiness probes, resource requests + limits, horizontal pod autoscaling, persistent storage, graceful shutdown. This week you make your cluster production-ready.
topics: Liveness, readiness, and startup probes — when each matters
Resource requests + limits — CPU and memory, what happens at OOMKill
QoS classes — Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler — scaling on CPU, on custom metrics
PersistentVolume + PersistentVolumeClaim — stateful workloads
StatefulSets — for stateful apps that need stable network IDs
